scenes.say: One server handles a thousand requests a second, then it falls over. You'll take it to a hundred thousand, defend every database choice, and answer the C A P question.
Today you will do three things. Scale one server to a hundred thousand requests a second. Choose a database and defend it. And answer what happens when the network splits.

scenes.title: One server, 100,000 req/s
scenes.statement: One app server maxes out at 1,000 requests a second. Traffic is 100,000. Scale it without logging users out.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. One server tops out at a thousand requests a second. For example, traffic is a hundred thousand. We want to serve all of it. And users must stay logged in.

scenes.head: One server vs the traffic
scenes.say: Here's why this matters. Interviewers love scaling, because it tests whether you measure first. One server tops out near a thousand requests a second. Your traffic is a hundred thousand. The order you fix things in is the answer.

scenes.head: A shop with a long line
scenes.say: A shop has a long line. You can hire a faster cashier, or open more checkouts. A faster cashier hits a limit. More checkouts keep growing, but share one warehouse. In your system, the warehouse is the database.

scenes.head: Vertical vs horizontal
scenes.say: Vertical means a bigger machine, horizontal means more machines. Good: vertical is simple, horizontal has no single point of failure. Limit: vertical hits a hardware ceiling, horizontal adds moving parts. Needs: horizontal needs a stateless app behind a load balancer.

scenes.head: Load balancer, identical copies
scenes.say: The load balancer spreads requests across identical copies of the app. Add a third copy, and capacity grows by a thousand requests a second. One copy dies, and traffic simply goes to the others.

scenes.head: Why stateless matters
scenes.say: Here's stateless, by breaking it. Each server keeps sessions in its own memory. Ana logs in on server A. The balancer sends her next request to server B. B has never heard of her. She's logged out.
Your turn. How do you fix it? Where should the session live, so that any server can read it? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Where should sessions live so any server works?

scenes.head: State lives outside the app
scenes.say: A shared store, like Redis. Now any server can read Ana's session. Sessions and cache live in Redis, durable data lives in the database. Kill a server and nobody is logged out.

scenes.title: One database, many servers
scenes.statement: Every app server hits one database. Reads and writes pile up on one machine.
scenes.say: New problem. A hundred app servers now share one database. For example, ten thousand queries a second reach it. We want it to keep up. And reads must stay fresh enough.

scenes.head: Replicas, and replica lag
scenes.say: App servers are easy to copy. The database is not. Writes go to one primary, which copies them to read replicas. A user posts a comment and refreshes. The replica hasn't caught up, so the comment is gone. That's replica lag. For your own fresh writes, read from the primary.

scenes.head: Sharding by user id
scenes.say: The primary can't keep up? You shard. Split rows across databases by a key. Here the key is user id, and the rule is user id modulo four. Seven goes to database three. Twelve goes to zero. Why user id? Millions of values, spread evenly.

output.text:
7 goes to db 3
12 goes to db 0
1001 goes to db 1

scenes.say: Your turn. You grow from four shards to five, and the rule becomes user id modulo five. Roughly what share of users stay on the same shard? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 4 shards to 5, with user_id % N. Share that stay?

scenes.head: Adding one shard
scenes.say: About twenty percent. The chart counts users who stay on their shard. The other eighty percent move. That's why shard counts are painful. Consistent hashing moves fewer.

scenes.head: Order of attack
scenes.say: So the order of attack. First, measure to find the bottleneck. Then cheap wins: indexes, a cache, queues, a C D N. Next, scale out the stateless app tier. Then read replicas. Shard last, because it adds permanent complexity.

scenes.head: Whiteboard math
scenes.say: Assume a thousand requests a second per app server. A hundred servers take the whole load. A cache absorbs ninety percent. Of the rest, eight thousand are reads, spread over four replicas. Two thousand writes hit the primary. Past that, shard four ways.

scenes.title: Mongo or Postgres?
scenes.statement: Pick a database for orders, and another for billions of event logs. Defend both picks.

example.output: a pick and a reason each

scenes.say: New problem. Pick a database for orders, and one for billions of event logs. For example, both. We want a pick and a reason for each. Start from access patterns.

scenes.head: Two ways to store an order
scenes.say: Mongo or Postgres? Start from access patterns, not favorites. Two ways to store orders. S Q L is linked spreadsheets: an orders sheet and an items sheet, joined by id. A document store keeps a folder per order, items inside.

items.label: Document store: a folder per order

scenes.head: Same order, two shapes
scenes.say: In S Q L, you join two tables to rebuild order seven. You get one row per item. In a document store, order seven is stored whole, items nested inside. One lookup reads it. Which product sold best across all orders? Easy in S Q L, awkward in documents.

panels.code:
SELECT o.id, i.sku, i.qty
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i
  ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.id = 7;

scenes.head: How to choose
scenes.say: Compare on five things. Shape: tables or documents. Relationships: joins are natural in S Q L. Transactions: strong across rows in S Q L. Scaling: S Q L goes up first, then replicas. Schema: enforced by the database, or by your code.
rows: duplicate, or look up in code

scenes.say: Your turn. A bank moves fifty dollars from one account to another. Both changes happen, or neither. Which store is the best default? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Money moves between accounts, all or nothing. Best default?

scenes.head: Match data to store
scenes.say: Postgres. Money needs all or nothing transactions. Event logs, billions of rows read by key, fit a document or wide column store. Carts and sessions are one lookup by key. Odd extra fields beside normal tables? Postgres has a JSONB type.

scenes.title: The network splits
scenes.statement: Two data centers lose contact, and a user reads from one of them. Answer with stale data, or refuse?

example.input: link down; x=2 written on A; read on B

scenes.say: Last problem. Two data centers lose contact. For example, a write lands on A, and a read lands on B. We want a clear answer: stale, or an error. You must pick one.

scenes.head: Two bank branches
scenes.say: Two bank branches share one account, balance one hundred. The phone line between them goes down. A customer withdraws forty at branch A. Branch B can't know. Someone asks B for the balance. Guess one hundred, or say come back later? That dilemma is the C A P theorem.

scenes.head: A partition: B must choose
scenes.say: Same thing with data. Replica A and replica B hold x, which is one. The link breaks. That's a partition, and it will happen eventually. A write arrives at A, setting x to two. A accepts it. Now a read arrives at B. B has exactly two choices.
Your turn. During the partition, B refuses to answer rather than risk a stale value. Which side of C A P did B choose? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: During a partition, B refuses to answer. It chose...

scenes.head: B has two choices
scenes.say: Consistency. B gives up availability to avoid a wrong answer. Choice one: B says x is one. Choice two: B waits until healed. Result: stale but up, or never stale with failed requests. Examples: Cassandra leans available, Zookeeper and etcd lean consistent.

scenes.head: Eventual consistency, healed
scenes.say: Availability-first systems offer eventual consistency. Each value carries a timestamp. A holds two at time five. B still says one. After the link heals, merge keeps the newest. Both now say two. Fine for likes and feeds, wrong for balances.

panels.code:
def merge(p, q):
    return max(p, q, key=lambda v: v[1])
a, b = (1, 0), (1, 0)
a = (2, 5)
print("B says", b[0])
m = merge(a, b)
a, b = m, m
print("healed", a[0], b[0])

scenes.head: CAP myths in interviews
scenes.say: Pick any two of three? No. In a partition you choose consistency or availability. Is eventual consistency bad? Fine for feeds, not balances. Conflicting writes? Last write wins can drop one. Version vectors detect it.
rows: Partitions happen: choose C or A during one
Last write wins, or version vectors

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do you scale a service? Measure, cache, go stateless, add replicas. Shard last. Why stateless? Any server can serve any request. Shard key? Many values, even spread, like user id.
rows: Measure, cache, scale out, replicas, shard last
Any server can serve any request
Many values, even spread: user id

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Which database? Postgres first. Move to No S Q L for scale or key access. Can Postgres store J S O N? Yes, JSONB. The mistake: choosing No S Q L because it's trendy.
rows: Postgres first; NoSQL for scale, key access

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Explain C A P. Partitions happen, so during one you choose consistency or availability. Eventual consistency? Replicas converge once writes stop. Fine for likes, not balances. Conflicting writes? Last write wins, or version vectors.
rows: In a partition: consistent or available

scenes.head: Build these next
scenes.say: Three exercises. Run two copies of a small web app, and move the sessions into Redis. Count how many ids move from four shards to five. Then explain C A P to a friend, using two bank branches.
So say this. Measure first, then cache, stateless servers, replicas, and shard last. Start with Postgres, and choose NoSQL for access patterns. In a partition, pick consistency or availability.
